chapter: Maynard Ferguson and the drinking life
title: Why booze and drugs go with jazz
summary: Time on buses and in clubs; drinking as an occupational hazard.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Is that — I’m trying to think how to phrase this question — that booze and so forth, and controlled substances and jazz, why is that almost considered to be —
Synonymous. Is it partly because you spent so much time on the bus and in hotel rooms and stuff and you have all this time on your hands? Or is it just like this —

Somebody once said that the only time a musician should drink is while he works, or when he’s working. But you’ve got so much time. You work four hours a day. I mean I hate to say work, play, because I’ve never worked a day in my life. But I mean you’re basically playing but I mean when you’re on the bus man, it’s party time. Like if you’re traveling and you’ve got an eight hour ride, what are you going to do? I mean sit there and — I mean some guys played cards, but most of us would be listening to music and getting drunk or getting high, and you burn it off on the bandstand. But it’s an occupational hazard. There’s no question about that.
Because often times you’re playing in places and you’re in a gin joint.
